# Introduction

Suppose we want to know how well people measure time. An accurate
reference timer runs an event for a few seconds, and two people, A and B,
each time it by hand. Their recorded times never match the actual duration
exactly. Part of the difference is just noise: a press a little early
here, a little late there. But part of it may belong to the person. If B
always presses a little late, B's times will run long by about the same
amount every time. In lecture, the astronomers called that steady personal
part the **personal equation**.

To separate the two, we need a rule that predicts a recorded time from
the actual duration **and** from who did the timing:

$$\text{recorded time} = \text{a part that grows with the actual duration} + \text{an adjustment for the observer} + \text{error}.$$

R's `lm()` fits exactly this kind of rule. Today you will fit it to
invented timings from A and B, and use the saved rule to answer: **when A
and B time an event of the same length, how much later does B record
than A?**

## Learning goals

In this lab, you will...

- write an `lm()` formula and save its model object;
- tell the model apart from its coefficient vector;
- use `predict()` to interpret a slope, an intercept, and a reference
  category, by changing one predictor and keeping the other fixed;
- plot the saved predictions and retrieve fitted values, residuals, and
  the SSE;
- check an AI tool's explanation of coefficients against your own
  predictions, following the course AI policy.

# Part 2 — Fit a model and find out what you saved

## The practice data

An accurate reference timer gives an event's actual duration. Two imagined
observers, A and B, record it. These **invented data** are the timing
experiment from the Introduction: a recorded measurement may depend on who
observes it. They are not historical records or measurements from this
class.

There are 20 rows, each one a single timing. Each observer records each of
five durations twice. `actual_s` and `recorded_s` are in seconds; `reading`
is a row identifier. A factor stores categories. Setting its levels to
`c("A", "B")` makes A the reference category under R's default coding.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
timing <- read_csv("data/observer_timing.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
timing <- timing |>
  mutate(observer = factor(observer, levels = c("A", "B")))
head(timing)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  reading actual_s observer recorded_s
    <dbl>    <dbl> <fct>         <dbl>
1       1        2 A              2.26
2       2        2 A              2.46
3       3        2 B              2.76
4       4        2 B              3.16
5       5        4 A              4.32
6       6        4 A              4.72
```


:::
:::


## Write the fit

The pattern is `model_name <- lm(response ~ predictor, data = table_name)`.
The response goes left of `~`; predictors go right. `<-` saves the returned
object. `lm()` includes an intercept by default and chooses coefficients to
minimize the sum of squared observed-minus-fitted differences.

Our first rule predicts recorded time using actual duration alone.
`coef(model_name)` retrieves its coefficients; typing the model's name
prints a short display of the fit.

**2.1** Fit `recorded_s ~ actual_s` using `timing`, save the model as
`fit_time`, and print both the model and `coef(fit_time)`. Write the fitted
equation using the two printed coefficients, in the form

predicted `recorded_s` = ___ + ___ × `actual_s`;

we will interpret them by making predictions in Part 3.

## The printed display is not the whole object

The saved model is a **list**, a container of named components, and
`names()` lists them. You can ignore most of them; notice `coefficients`,
`fitted.values`, and `residuals`. You already used `$` to extract a column
from a table; it also extracts a component of a list. For example,
`fit_time$coefficients` retrieves the same numbers as `coef(fit_time)`.
Use `coef()` for your calculations.

Do not overwrite the model with its coefficients. A coefficient vector does
not retain everything `predict()` needs, such as the model formula and
information about factor levels.

**2.2** Save `coef(fit_time)` as `b` and print it, then run
`names(fit_time)`. How does `b` differ from `fit_time`?

# Part 3 — Interpret a slope by changing one thing

`predict(fit_time, newdata = new_rows)` applies the **saved** rule to
the rows of a new table. It does not fit another model. The table must have
a predictor column named `actual_s`; it does not need `recorded_s`, because
that is what you want to predict.

`predict()` returns a numeric vector, one prediction per new row, in the
same order. For a vector `p`, `p[1]` selects its first value;
`p[2] - p[1]` calculates the second prediction minus the first.

**3.1** Create rows at 4 and 5 actual seconds. Save their predictions
as `p_time`, print them, and calculate the second minus the first. Between
the two rows, how much did the actual time, `actual_s`, change? How much
did the predicted recorded time change? Compare that change with
`b["actual_s"]`. What does the slope tell you happens to the predicted
recorded time when the actual time goes up by one second?

**3.2** Use `predict()` at `actual_s = 0` and compare the prediction with
`b["(Intercept)"]`. What does the intercept predict, and is zero inside the
observed range of 2–10 seconds?

# Part 4 — Add an observer, then change one predictor at a time

The formula `recorded_s ~ actual_s + observer` is the rule from the
Introduction: a part that grows with actual duration, plus an adjustment
for the observer. Its rule is:

```text
predicted recorded time = intercept + duration slope × actual duration
                         + B adjustment (only when observer is B)
```

The `+` gives an additive rule: the same duration slope for both observers,
plus a constant B-minus-A adjustment. The first factor level, A, is the
reference. We will use predictions to find out what each coefficient means.
Do not refit the model between comparisons.

Replacing `+` with `*`, as in `recorded_s ~ actual_s * observer`, adds an
**interaction**: each observer gets their own duration slope, so the
B-minus-A gap can change with duration. Today we use only the additive
rule.

**4.1** Fit `recorded_s ~ actual_s + observer` using `timing`, save it
as `fit_observer`, and save its coefficients as `b_observer`. Print the
coefficients. How many are there, and which coefficient name is new?

## Make pairs that differ in one column

This model needs **both** predictor columns in `newdata`: `actual_s` and
`observer`. You may supply the known observer labels as text; R checks them
against the factor levels used in the fit. Use the same column names and
labels as in the fitting data.

Compare rows before subtracting their predictions. To interpret a duration
coefficient, keep observer fixed. To interpret an observer coefficient,
keep duration fixed.

**4.2** Predict for the four rows below and save the vector as
`p_observer`. Calculate all four differences in your document's
skeleton. For each, name what changed and what stayed fixed. Compare the
duration differences with `b_observer["actual_s"]` and the observer
differences with `b_observer["observerB"]`. Interpret both coefficients
with units.
(The duration slope is in recorded seconds per actual second; the B
adjustment is in seconds.)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
comparison_rows <- tibble(
  actual_s = c(4, 5, 4, 5),
  observer = c("A", "A", "B", "B")
)
```
:::


**4.3** Make two rows at actual duration zero, one for A and one for B,
and predict for both. Which prediction equals `b_observer["(Intercept)"]`,
and why does the intercept refer to A?

# Part 5 — Plot the predictions and retrieve the residuals

## Plot the saved rule

`expand.grid()` makes every combination of the supplied values. Here it
makes ten rows: five durations for each of two observers. Add predictions
from the saved model, then draw the lines with `geom_line()`. This displays
the model you already fitted; the plotting code does not fit a new one.

In the plot, the point layer uses `timing`. The line layer uses
`prediction_grid`, keeps the x mapping, and replaces the y mapping with
the prediction column. Color and line type group the predictions by observer.

**5.1** In your document, fill in the prediction call and the line
layer, then run the plot. How do the slope and vertical separation of the
two lines show the two comparisons you made in 4.2?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prediction_grid <- expand.grid(
  actual_s = seq(2, 10, by = 2),
  observer = c("A", "B")
)
```
:::


## Retrieve results for the fitting rows

`fitted(fit_observer)` returns predictions for the original fitting rows.
`resid(fit_observer)` returns observed minus fitted for those same rows.
Both are numeric vectors in fitting-row order. Here the data have no missing
values and have not been reordered or filtered, so we can attach the vectors
to `timing`. Do not attach them to a different table of new rows.

**5.2** Create `timing_results` by adding `fitted_s` and `residual_s`
from `fit_observer` to `timing`, and print the first four rows. Check that
the first residual is observed minus fitted, then calculate the training
SSE with `sum(resid(fit_observer)^2)`. How do `fitted()` and
`predict(..., newdata = ...)` differ in which rows they describe?

# Part 6 — AI explains; you check

The course
[syllabus](https://statistical-history.github.io/syllabus.html) lets you
use AI to ask coding questions or debug code. **First make a genuine
attempt yourself**, then verify and revise what the tool gives you. You
have made that attempt: in Part 4 you interpreted all three coefficients
of `fit_observer` from your own predictions. Now see whether an AI tool
reads them the same way.

**Do not copy and paste a prompt** from these instructions; formulate your
own question.

**6.1** In your own words, ask an AI tool of your choice to explain what
each of the three coefficients of `fit_observer` means. Give it what it
needs: the formula, the printed coefficients, what each column means and
its units, and that A is the reference observer. In your document, record
your request, the tool and model, the date, and a link to the
conversation, and quote the AI's explanation of each coefficient.

**6.2** Check each explanation against the predictions you made in 4.2
and 4.3. For each coefficient, does the AI's explanation match your
predictions: the difference between two predictions for the slope and the
B adjustment, and the prediction for A at 0 seconds for the intercept?
Quote any sentence that is wrong, or that
claims more than the predictions show, for example a reason *why* B
records later, or calling the intercept an average. Answer in your own
words, not with AI.

# R reference

| Task | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Fit and save | `fit <- lm(y ~ x + group, data = dat)` |
| List a model's components | `names(fit)` |
| Extract coefficients | `b <- coef(fit)` |
| Select a coefficient by name | `b["x"]` |
| Predict chosen rows | `p <- predict(fit, newdata = new_rows)` |
| Compare two rows | `p[2] - p[1]` |
| Retrieve fitting-row results | `fitted(fit)`; `resid(fit)` |
| Calculate training SSE | `sum(resid(fit)^2)` |

Use `?lm` and `?predict.lm` in RStudio, or the official help pages for
[`lm()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/lm.html)
and
[`predict.lm()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/predict.lm.html).
